Peut-on s’armer contre la violence conju: Can you arm yourself against intimate partner violence?
Tout a été brisé : la confiance, l’estim: Everything was broken: trust, self-esteem. You have to rework it all,” says Cassandra.
Nancy a subi la violence conjugale seule: Nancy endured intimate partner violence alone. She never went to the police or to a support worker.
« C’était ma première relation, je n’ava: “It was my first relationship, I had nothing to compare it to,” says the woman, who was 15 when it all began. “My boyfriend was a sweetheart with everyone, but as soon as we closed the door at home, it was hell,” recalls Nancy, who chose not to share her last name to protect herself and her children. That hell lasted 10 years and ended with the suicide of her violent partner.
Du moins, cet enfer a en partie pris fin: Or at least, it partly ended, because the young mother took years to get back on her feet and to realize what she had been through. “I knew that what had happened had hurt me, because I fell into a depression after his death, but not to that extent,” she continues. When she told her story to an aunt, the aunt said: “Why didn’t you come to me? This is awful!”
Pourquoi ne s’est-elle pas fait aider ?: Why didn’t she get help? “I had learned to fend for myself, I didn’t even realize I needed help,” she continues. Nancy is far from the only one to have made it through without help, in the solitude and isolation that come with intimate partner violence. She is also not the only one to have been trapped by her relationship.
Au Québec, une femme sur cinq est victim: In Quebec, one in five women experiences intimate partner violence in her lifetime. And among them, some pay with their lives, like Rebekah Harry, murdered by her partner on March 23. At 29, she became the seventh woman to die at the hands of her partner since the start of 2021.
Chaque histoire de violence conjugale es: Every story of intimate partner violence is different; each one reveals a new facet. And it is this diversity that makes it so hard to detect. “It’s impossible to spot the first signs of intimate partner violence. Everyone makes mistakes in life,” Claudine Thibaudeau, clinical support manager and spokesperson for SOS violence conjugale, reassures us.
« La victime est noyée dans la manipulat: “The victim is drowning in manipulation. It creates a kind of fiction. Intimate partner violence is hard to see for what it is,” she explains. Women who call SOS violence conjugale often downplay what is happening to them, Thibaudeau adds.
<strong>La violence conjugale n’est pas: Intimate partner violence is not only physical
Démystifier l’idée de la femme battue, v: Demystifying the idea of the battered woman is the challenge facing support workers: intimate partner violence is invisible and therefore undetectable. In their interventions and in shelters, they all work to make women aware of the many forms this violence takes. Many actions and behaviours leave no marks but are violent.
« Il faut montrer que la violence conjug: “We have to show that intimate partner violence isn’t just physical!” and “Just because you have no bruises doesn’t mean you’re not experiencing intimate partner violence,” the women we spoke to repeated, one after another.Cassandra* is a special education technician specializing in mental health and intimate partner violence. Her experience did not protect her from her toxic relationship, from which she is still trying to heal. She met her abuser in June. As in most cases, the violence didn’t appear overnight, and her partner wasn’t violent from the first date. “At first, he was nice; it was a great meeting,” she says.
Peu à peu, il se révèle jaloux, la harcè: Little by little, he revealed himself to be jealous, harassed her, invaded her apartment, controlled her physical appearance and who she spent time with, isolated her from her loved ones and family, spied on her and monitored her. “I stopped washing, I stopped eating; I lost seven pounds. I no longer take the same route to work. It takes so long to recover. Everything was broken: trust, self-esteem. You have to rework it all,” says Cassandra. Today, months later, she is still on sick leave due to post-traumatic shock.Intimate partner violence isn’t limited to blows.
Elle est aussi verbale, économique, sexu: It is also verbal, economic, sexual and psychological. And in that last form, intangible, it settles in slowly and insidiously. And it can become among the most brutal and devastating for the victim.
<strong>Violence conjugale ou dispute de: Intimate partner violence or a couple’s quarrel?
Grâce à leur expérience, les intervenant: Thanks to their experience, support workers have some pointers to help the women who come to see them. “You have to look at the intention behind the argument. Is it always him who wins?” explains Roxane Prénovost, coordinator at La Passe-R-Elle, a support and shelter home in the Hautes-Laurentides. Is the intention to belittle the other person, or simply to talk in order to resolve a conflict? “In a fight, violent words and actions are spontaneous.
Dans un cas de violence conjugale, ils s: In a case of intimate partner violence, they’re intentional. There’s a desire for control and domination,” Prénovost continues.The second thing to look at, to tell them apart, is the effect. “With intimate partner violence, the victim is afraid of the other person’s reactions. What consequences do I risk, even if it’s not physical? You don’t apologize, you justify yourself,” the coordinator explains, stressing that it is never normal to be afraid of your partner.
Mieux comprendre la violence conjugale,: Understanding intimate partner violence better also means understanding that it occurs in cycles: tension, violent act, apologies and reconciliation. “He told me I was the only person who mattered, but called me stupid every day,” Nancy continues. This violence forced her to justify herself, to apologize and to blame herself.
Elle raconte qu’un jour, son ancien conj: She recounts that one day, her violent ex-partner exploded after she spent an afternoon chatting with an ex at the village carnival: “I was devastated, I wanted to disappear. How could I have been so cruel to him?
Je me suis excusée sans arrêt, je voulai: I apologized non-stop, I wanted so badly for him to forgive me for being so careless and for hurting him so much.” The insults subsided, the tension eased. They talked and reconciled. But it didn’t last and, as always, the tensions returned.
« Ce cycle laisse croire que la femme es: “This cycle makes it seem like the woman is always at fault. The honeymoon phase feeds the hope that things will improve. And that’s normal, because you fell in love with your partner,” Prénovost sums up. The women we met insist on one thing: “You shouldn’t be ashamed.”According to Prénovost, women are socialized to take things on themselves and adapt to the other person’s needs and anger.
« Sauver le couple est aussi quelque cho: “Saving the couple is also something we carry on our shoulders,” the coordinator continues, in an effort to relieve victims of guilt. In a context of violence, it can seem easier to accept, to tolerate and to say nothing than to confront the other person and risk reprisals.
Il faut en moyenne sept ou huit ruptures: It takes an average of seven or eight breakups to leave a toxic relationship for good. Watching this situation helplessly can be very frustrating for friends and family, but they need to stay. “Loved ones are a source of power. The less isolated the victim is, the safer she is,” advises Claudine Thibaudeau of SOS violence conjugale.“Giving power back to women” is, for her, the key piece of advice in a situation of intimate partner violence.
Elle et son équipe travaillent donc à me: She and her team therefore work to put words to what women are going through, to equip them and to give them choices.“Often, the first reflex of loved ones is to make the woman experiencing violence realize that she shouldn’t tolerate the situation,” says Thibaudeau. They want to do everything to get her out of the cycle and bring her to leave her violent partner. Here, Thibaudeau calls for caution: “If I force her to adopt my view of the situation, I’m behaving violently too.”
Elle conseille donc de respecter le ryth: She therefore advises respecting the victim’s pace, accompanying and supporting her, rather than telling her what to do. It is the best way to give power back. “You have to give choices, not solutions,” she continues.
« Il faut arrêter de juger les femmes ba: “We have to stop judging battered women who stay! When it comes to intimate partner violence, we’re all alone. Honestly, if he were still alive, I wouldn’t be at peace,” Nancy implores. The mother adds that she wishes she could have talked about it, to understand that her former boyfriend had no right to control how she dressed and who she spent time with.
« J’aurais été capable de reprendre le c: “I would have been able to take back control,” she says. That is what she tries to pass on to those around her, especially young people.Another fundamental piece of advice for loved ones is to think about the victim’s safety. “There’s a false belief that if the woman leaves, she’ll be safe. But that’s not always the case. It can sometimes happen years later,” reports Claudine Thibaudeau of SOS violence conjugale.
Dans bien des cas de violence conjugale,: In many cases of intimate partner violence, separation does not mean liberation. The woman can be at greatest risk after the breakup. “If a woman hesitates to leave, it’s because she knows she’ll be in more danger once she leaves her partner,” explains Thibaudeau.
Au-delà des violences directes de l’ex-c: Beyond the direct violence from the ex-partner, there is the weight of the judicial and legal process, as well as the psychological aftereffects of the toxic relationship. You can leave a situation of intimate partner violence and remain traumatized for years.
Il aura fallu 20 ans à Nancy pour ne plu: It took Nancy 20 years to no longer “feel like crying.”
Sa fille, la plus âgée de ses enfants, p: Her daughter, the eldest of her children, still bears the absence of a father’s love she never knew. “You don’t heal from intimate partner violence,” said all the women who have experienced intimate partner violence whom we met.For Nancy, as for the others, the fact that intimate partner violence brands a life like a hot iron doesn’t mean we shouldn’t do everything to fight it.
